title: Ain’t nobody better: Chaka Khan’s 20 best songs – ranked!
text:
20. Love You All My Lifetime (1992)
Chaka Khan had harsh words for the “assholes” at her then record company, Warner Bros, who she felt under-promoted 1992’s The Woman I Am, her first album in four years. Listening to Love You All My Lifetime’s cocktail of funk and contemporary R&B, you wonder if she didn’t have a point. There’s no obvious reason why it wasn’t huge hit.
19. Hello Happiness (2019)
Dissatisfied with her treatment by various record labels and managers, Khan released albums with less frequency in the 21st century – which made 2019’s Hello Happiness (and its title track) feel like a comeback. Producer Switch clearly knew what to do, the songwriting was strong, Khan’s voice still sizzles.
18. Any Old Sunday (1981)
A deep cut nestled in the middle of her best solo album, What ’Cha Gonna Do for Me, Any Old Sunday is easily overlooked amid the bigger hitters, but offers three-and- a-half minutes of instant sunshine: carefree mid-tempo disco funk – a hint of Chic about the guitars – with a vocal that adds heft to the poppy melody.
17. Through the Fire (1984)
I Feel for You was the smash, but the biggest streaming song from the album of the same name is, by some distance, Through the Fire. Perhaps because Kanye West sampled it on Through the Wire; perhaps because Khan brings an earthy power to a glossy, but classy, adult contemporary ballad.
16. Spoon (1998)
The most unfairly overlooked album in Khan’s catalogue is Come 2 My House, a collaboration with Prince that had the misfortune to be released when his commercial standing was in the doldrums, despite the fact that he could still turn out funk as sensual and weird as Spoon. But it’s not on streaming; someone rerelease it!
15. Rufus – At Midnight (My Love Will Lift You Up) (ft Chaka Khan) (1977)
The sessions for Ask Rufus were turbulent – drummer Andre Fischer and Khan’s then husband, Richard Holland, had a punch-up in the studio – but you’d never guess from the Chicago band’s fifth album. At Midnight is its solitary dancefloor-focused track, but its understated funk is the perfect setting for Khan’s compelling switches from softness to raunch.
14. Rufus – You Got the Love (ft Chaka Khan) (1974)
Rufus’s debut album was promising, but unfocussed, not least in the fact that it kept allowing Khan to cede the microphone. But on its follow-up, Rags to Rufus, everything snapped into place. Opener You Got the Love offers thrillingly gritty funk – the perfect counterpoint to lush Philly soul – and Chaka in full effect.
13. Rufus & Chaka – Any Love (1979)
Khan might have been contractually obliged to keep recording with Rufus, despite her solo success, but 1979’s Masterjam doesn’t feel like an album made under duress. Any Love is tough, disco-paced, subtly orchestrated and entirely fantastic, Khan telling a predatory ladies’ man how pathetic she thinks he is in no uncertain terms.
12. Chaka Khan and Rufus – Stay (1978)
For all the endless turmoil in their ranks – the band’s lineup seemed to change constantly – Rufus and Khan made music that sounded absolutely effortless. The Khan-co-written big hit from their sixth album, Street Player, is a case in point. It’s an extremely cool breeze, which just makes Khan’s vaulting raw vocal seem all the more potent.
11. Rufus – Once You Get Started (ft Chaka Khan) (1974)
Boosted by the platinum-selling success of Rags to Rufus, 1974’s Rufusized was a supremely confident album. With one eye on the burgeoning disco scene, opener Once You Get Started sands down some of its predecessor’s rough edges, but its chattering, synth-laden call to the dancefloor is impossible to resist.
10. Rufus & Chaka – Do You Love What You Feel (1979)
Fresh from collaborating with Khan on his superb 1978 single Stuff Like That, Quincy Jones brought a dose of production sophistication to Rufus’s Masterjam album. His sleek touch is all over the joy-bringing Do You Love What You Feel, a perfect platform for Khan’s exuberant vocal: “I wanna dance all night!”
9. Papillon (AKA Hot Butterfly) (1980)
Mid-tempo disco so wistful and sad it could cause an outbreak of ugly crying on the dancefloor: Khan sounds fantastic, especially backed by Luther Vandross. The original version, by writer Gregg Diamond’s Bionic Boogie, with a lead vocal from Vandross himself and a 12in mix by Jim Burgess, might be even better.
8. Fate (1981)
These days, Fate is hard to listen to without automatically thinking of the more famous track that sampled it: Stardust’s Music Sounds Better With You. But temporarily banish the thought of French touch house from your brain and luxuriate instead in the original’s glorious update of disco for the 80s. It’s a treat.
7. Rufus – Tell Me Something Good (1974)
You didn’t need to read the credits to work out that Rufus’s breakthough hit was the handiwork of Stevie Wonder: its reggae-influenced groove and vocodered backing vocals could have stepped straight off Innervisions or Talking Book. But, barely into her 20s, Khan sounds entirely in charge, her voice totally commanding.
6. Clouds (1980)
A Paradise Garage classic, Ashford and Simpson’s Clouds is a disco monster, shifting from a dramatic opening verse that never quite goes where you expect to a headily euphoric chorus, complete with sound effects and a wild guitar solo. Pub quiz fact: it also features a 16-year-old Whitney Houston on backing vocals.
5. I Know You, I Live You (1981)
The highlight of What Cha’ Gonna Do for Me, co-penned by producer Arif Mardin and Khan, with the latter presumably responsible for the slightly odd, I-will-manifest-a-relationship lyrics. It is beautifully executed post-disco boogie – check Average White Band drummer Steve Ferrone’s superb rhythm track – with a wonderful melody and a frankly awesome performance from Khan herself.
4. Rufus – Sweet Thing (ft Chaka Khan) (1975)
A Top 5 US hit, Sweet Thing is the go-to Rufus slow jam, its distinctive guitar riff later borrowed by Nile Rodgers for David Bowie’s hit version of China Girl (you can definitely hear the similarity). Worth a mention is Mary J Blige’s superb, subtly updated 1992 cover, best heard in its scuffed-up remix version.
3. I Feel for You (1984)
Previously recorded by its author, Prince, and by the Pointer Sisters (and subsequently by Mickey Mouse Club-era Britney Spears and Justin Timberlake), Khan’s version is the definitive reading. An ultra-catchy song in any version, her vocal cuts through the none-more-mid-80s production to create a slice of electronic funk that’s genuinely timeless.
2. I’m Every Woman (1978)
The song for which Khan is most likely to be remembered has been variously rendered as reggae, house music, bossa nova and smooth jazz – sampled umpteen times and covered by Aretha Franklin and Whitney Houston. But look beyond its ubiquity, and marvel at the climactic key changes and Khan’s ferocious vocal performance.
1. Rufus and Chaka Khan – Ain’t Nobody (1983)
One of the greatest singles of the 80s began life on a contract-fulfilling slate of studio tracks, appended to the live Stompin’ at the Savoy record. Khan had already left Rufus and had to be coaxed back for one last album. But Ain’t Nobody was a synth-funk masterpiece that transcended its unpromising beginnings. An eagle-eared Quincy Jones suggested Michael Jackson might want the song for Thriller, but Rufus and producer David “Hawk” Wolinski rebuffed him. It’s hard to see how even Jackson could have improved on the group’s version, with its impossibly infectious synth line, air of nocturnal anticipation and Khan’s vocal, which really doesn’t sound like the work of a woman heading for the door.
